text:
Bulk classification and decision inference on one GPU. spinf-serve reads a piece of content once and answers many questions about it in the same pass. Each answer is a probability over the options you give, not generated text. It runs on one 24 GB NVIDIA GPU and serves an OpenAI-compatible API, the same API as the hosted spinf service. Apache 2.0. We built this engine for our own work: a daily market index read from millions of news articles, each article asked dozens of narrow, calibrated questions. A serving engine built for chat re-reads the content for every question and generates one token at a time, which made that job slow and expensive. spinf-serve lays every question out as a branch of one read of the content and packs many contents into one forward pass. Bulk classification is where it started and where it is strongest. The same mechanism is what is now called a decision model : a model that returns a probability over a fixed set of answers (yes or no, a label, a level) instead of a paragraph. Any open instruction model works this way in spinf-serve, and dedicated decision models run as they are. The hosted spinf API grew out of this engine; we are publishing it because people asked to run it on their own hardware. It is not a chat server. Nothing is generated unless you ask for it, and it is built for throughput rather than for the latency of a single request. Linux, an NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB and fp8 tensor cores (Ada, Hopper or Blackwell: RTX 4090 / 5090, L4, L40S, RTX 6000 Ada, H100), a driver supporting CUDA 13, Python 3.12. Ampere cards run with int8 weights instead ( configuration ). pip install " spinf-serve[server] " spinf-serve serve spinf/gemma-4-12b-fp8 # downloads the checkpoint on first start; serves on port 8000 Or the image, with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed (the volume keeps the model and the compile caches; arguments after the image name are those of spinf-serve serve ): docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 -v spinf-cache:/root/.cache ghcr.io/spinfinc/spinf-serve Then ask. Two classifications and one extraction from a single read of the content: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/score \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' { "model": "spinf/gemma-4-12b-fp8", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Customer support message:
I was charged twice for September, please refund one of the charges." } ], "scoring": { "queries": [ { "id": "topic", "template": "

Topic (billing, technical, account, shipping, or cancellation):{?}", "options": [" billing", " technical", " account", " shipping", " cancellation"] }, { "id": "refund", "template": "

Is the customer asking for a refund?
Answer:{?}", "options": [" yes", " no"] }, { "id": "month", "template": "

Q: Which month was charged twice?
A: "{*}"" } ] } } ' For each scored question the response gives every option's probability, and the same probability on empty content (real numbers from the 12B model): { "id" : " refund " , "combinations" : [ { "values" : {}, "options" : [ { "text" : " yes " , "logprob" : -0.90 , "p" : 0.72 , "floor_p" : 0.60 }, { "text" : " no " , "logprob" : -1.86 , "p" : 0.28 , "floor_p" : 0.40 } ], "residual" : 0.44 } ] } p is the probability among your options. floor_p is the same question with no content, so p - floor_p is what the content added (here topic moves " billing" from 0.47 to 0.91). residual is the probability that went to words outside your options. For month the response lists the most likely answers with their probabilities ("September" first). The same body, with an API key, runs against api.spinf.com ; the OpenAI SDKs work through /v1/chat/completions with the scoring block in extra_body ( quickstart ). Measured on one RTX 4090 with Gemma 4 12B in fp8: 24 Wikinews articles of about 470 tokens, 56 two-option questions each, 1,344 questions in all (the public job set in fixtures/ ), sent over HTTP to spinf-serve and to vLLM 0.26 with prefix caching. The script and the full results are in benchmarks/ . vLLM already reuses each article across its 56 questions through the prefix cache. What it cannot do is answer them in one forward pass: it runs 1,344 single-token requests, while spinf-serve lays the 56 questions out as branches of one read and packs the 24 articles into two 16k-token passes. The gap grows with the number of questions per content. In practice, per 4090 with the 12B model: the spinf/moderation pack (106 questions per message, 22 categories) scores about 20,000 messages per hour; a news article asked 74 questions is read at nearly 700 questions per second. Extraction slots add decoding work (a searched slot costs about as much as 200 to 600 tokens of scoring, a generated one up to about 2,000) but share the read. A job is rarely one question: content moderation is 106 of them, each calibrated against normal traffic and combined into category scores and a decision. A prompt pack is one file holding the questions, how the content is presented to the model, how the answers turn into scores and how the scores turn into a decision. The server preloads packs and a request names one ( "packs": [{"id": "spinf/moderation"}] ), getting the pack's categories and decision back next to its own questions, from the same read. The official packs are in spinf-prompts , loaded by default. The server loads packs from any GitHub repository or local folder given with --packs ; PACKS.md lists every pack we know of , ours and others', and an issue adds yours. Format, request fields and sources: docs/prompt-packs.md . Each is a checkpoint we quantized and calibrated, published on the Hugging Face Hub with its recipe ( quantizations/ ); the engine pins the revision it was parity-tested on. Any other Hub checkpoint of a supported architecture family runs by its path, quantized at load time. docs/ : quickstart , examples , scoring API , configuration , writing questions , calibration , prompt packs , FAQ ; the guides (decision models, probabilities you can act on, few-shot classification, sentiment, survey coding, moderation, intent routing); and the engineering documents on how the engine works ( architecture , batch invariance , precision , the Qwen stack , extraction ). Version 0.1. The engine (scoring, extraction, generation, media, batch invariance, the two model stacks) is complete and parity-tested against recorded references; the server speaks the public API of the hosted service; the four checkpoints are public. What is still missing is listed in docs/README.md . Questions, ideas and bugs go to the issues of this repository. There is no forum or chat, and nothing is too small. spinf_serve/ holds the engine ( protocol , compiler , packer , scorer , extract , service ), the served models' manifests, the packs module (pure Python, also used by the client and the hosted API), one model stack per architecture family in models/ , the quantization schemes in quant/ , the HTTP server in server/ and the spinf-serve command. quantizations/ has one folder per published checkpoint (recipe, calibration output, model card), fixtures/ the public parity fixture and references, benchmarks/ the throughput comparison. The map of the code is docs/ARCHITECTURE.md . uv sync --extra server uv run pytest # CPU tests (the official packs' golden fixtures need ../spinf-prompts or SPINF_PROMPTS_DIR) uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 uv run spinf-serve parity --fixture fixtures/wikinews_20261024.json.gz \ --reference fixtures/wikinews_20261024.spinf-gemma-4-12b-fp8.json.gz --passes 2 Every change that touches a kernel, a compile boundary or a quantization scheme ships with the GPU parity run: bit-identical log-probabilities on the recorded reference of each published checkpoint ( fixtures/ ). Dependencies are pinned exactly; they change only together with a parity run. See CONTRIBUTING.md . Apache 2.0 ( LICENSE , NOTICE ). The models we run and re-quantize, the projects we build on, the techniques we implement and the data we checked on are credited in ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md .
